Newly hatched individuals of the duck leech, Theromyzon tessulatum, emerge from their cocoons at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0003 grams [Wwb = 0.0003 grams]. This minuscule starting mass reflects the limited yolk reserves provisioned within each egg and imposes a substantial challenge for the lecithotrophic larva as it transitions to exogenous feeding. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the interval between egg deposition and eclosion spans approximately 27.0 days [ab = approximately 27.0 days]. This developmental period is comparatively extended relative to other freshwater rhynchobdellid leeches of similar ultimate body size, likely owing to the relatively low metabolic rates typical of the genus Theromyzon during embryonic stages. Following eclosion, the juvenile leeches commence active feeding on the mucous membranes and blood of aquatic birds, initiating a phase of rapid somatic growth that ultimately carries them toward reproductive competence.

As the juveniles of Theromyzon tessulatum grow, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic development before attaining reproductive maturity. In specimens reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 120.0 days [tp = 120.0 days], a duration that reflects the substantial accumulation of body mass necessary to support gametogenesis and subsequent reproductive effort. Upon reaching this developmental milestone, individuals exhibit a wet weight at puberty of 0.25 grams [Wwp = 0.25 grams], which is notably identical to the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults. This convergence of pubertal and asymptotic mass is unusual among leeches and suggests that, in this species, the onset of reproductive capability coincides with the completion of structural growth, after which further increases in body size are minimal. The attainment of sexual maturity at this size likely represents an energetic threshold whereby stored resources become sufficient to fuel the production of the large, yolky eggs characteristic of the genus.

Reproductive output in Theromyzon tessulatum is considerable for an animal of its modest dimensions. When maintained at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a single female can deposit up to 200.0 eggs  during a single breeding episode, a fecundity that places this species among the more prolific members of the family Glossiphoniidae. Each egg is enclosed within a protective cocoon, and the entire clutch is brooded on the ventral surface of the parent until eclosion, a behaviour that enhances offspring survival but imposes significant energetic costs on the brooding adult. The large number of propagules per reproductive event is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over per-offspring investment, a pattern often observed in temporary or unpredictable aquatic habitats where juvenile mortality rates are elevated.

The overall lifespan of Theromyzon tessulatum, as recorded in captivity at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], reaches a maximum of 200.0 days [am = 200.0 days], a relatively brief duration that classifies this leech as an annual or short-lived iteroparous species. This longevity is somewhat shorter than that reported for several congeneric species inhabiting more stable thermal regimes, suggesting that the duck leech's life cycle is tightly synchronized with the seasonal availability of its waterfowl hosts. Throughout its adult phase, the reproductively viable organism may engage in multiple breeding events, although the window for reproduction is compressed by the brevity of its post-pubertal existence. Physiological deterioration becomes evident after approximately 180 days, with individuals showing reduced feeding activity and declining body condition, ultimately culminating in senescence and natural mortality before the 200-day mark is reached.

Ecologically, Theromyzon tessulatum occupies a specialized niche as a temporary ectoparasite of anatid birds, and its life-history schedule is finely tuned to the migratory phenology of its hosts. The duck leech achieves its ultimate wet weight of 0.25 grams [Wwi = 0.25 grams] within the first 60 to 80 days post-hatching when feeding conditions are optimal, a growth trajectory that enables it to parasitize waterfowl during the critical nesting season. Field surveys indicate that populations in northern temperate wetlands experience a single annual cohort, with cocoons deposited in early summer and juveniles overwintering in the sediment before resuming development the following spring. This seasonal synchrony underscores the ecological constraints under which the species operates; any mismatch between leech phenology and host arrival can drastically reduce feeding opportunities and, consequently, reproductive success.
